Molecular Basis of Cancer: Role of Genetic and Epigenetic Alterations

faq.a: A single activating mutation can drive cell growth, so the altered allele dominates over the normal one.
Yes; most cancers acquire multiple hits, often an oncogene plus loss of p53 or Rb.
faq.q: Can a tumour have both oncogene activation and tumor‑suppressor loss?

faq.a: It guides choice of affordable therapies (e.g., hormone vs chemotherapy) and informs screening for infection‑related cancers.
faq.q: What is the practical use of knowing a tumour’s molecular profile in a low‑resource hospital?

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with a breast lump is HER2‑negative on IHC – what next step and why? — Explain that HER2‑negative excludes trastuzumab; assess ER/PR status to decide hormone therapy.
A patient with colorectal cancer tests KRAS‑mutant – which targeted drug should be avoided and why? — EGFR antibodies are ineffective; explain mechanism of resistance.

You see a young man with a liver mass and chronic hepatitis B – which molecular mechanism is most likely and how does it affect management? — HBV DNA integration disrupts p53; antiviral therapy and surveillance are indicated.

A child from a schistosomiasis‑endemic area presents with bladder tumour – what infection‑related pathway should you consider? — Chronic inflammation leading to p53 loss; emphasize need for anti‑schistosomal treatment.

In a resource‑limited setting, you cannot perform PCR for EGFR – how would you decide on EGFR‑targeted therapy? — Use clinical clues (non‑smoker, adenocarcinoma histology) and consider empirical therapy only if affordable.
A patient on PD‑1 inhibitor develops severe colitis – what is the next step and why? — Stop immunotherapy, start high‑dose steroids; explain immune‑related adverse event management.
Explain why loss of p16INK4a is a useful diagnostic marker in HPV‑related cancers. — p16 over‑expression reflects Rb pathway disruption by HPV E7; aids in confirming viral etiology.

During ward rounds you notice a tumour with high Ki‑67 but low grade on histology – how do you reconcile and what does it mean for prognosis? — High proliferation suggests aggressive behaviour despite low grade; plan closer follow‑up.
ai.title: Molecular Basis of Cancer
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Cancer arises from genetic and epigenetic changes that disrupt normal cell growth control. Understanding oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and hallmarks of cancer guides diagnosis and therapy, especially where resources are limited.

b: Hallmarks: self‑sufficiency, evading growth suppressors, resisting death, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis
Most cancers result from multiple hits over years
sections.p: Cancer is a disease of uncontrolled cell proliferation caused by alterations in DNA that affect growth‑regulating pathways. The key concepts are oncogenes (gain‑of‑function) and tumor suppressor genes (loss‑of‑function).

b: Cyclin D–CDK4/6 drives G1→S; inhibited by p16INK4a
p53 induces p21 to halt cycle; loss leads to unchecked division
sections.p: Normal cells follow the cell‑cycle checkpoints (G1, S, G2, M) controlled by cyclins, CDKs, and checkpoint proteins. DNA damage triggers p53‑mediated apoptosis or repair; growth factors activate Ras‑MAPK and PI3K‑AKT pathways.
Gene expression is regulated at DNA, RNA, and protein levels. Epigenetic mechanisms (DNA methylation, histone modification) silence tumor suppressors; microRNAs fine‑tune oncogene translation.

b: HPV E6/E7 inactivate p53 and Rb → cervical, anal cancers
HBV DNA integration disrupts p53 → hepatocellular carcinoma
Schistosoma haematobium → bladder cancer via chronic inflammation
sections.p: Mutations, viral integration, chronic inflammation, and environmental carcinogens produce oncogenic activation or tumor‑suppressor loss. In low‑resource settings, infections (HPV, EBV, HBV, HCV, HIV) are major contributors.

b: KRAS mutation predicts resistance to EGFR antibodies in colorectal cancer
BRCA1/2 loss suggests benefit from PARP inhibitors
sections.p: Molecular alterations dictate prognosis, guide targeted therapy, and inform screening. In settings without advanced testing, clinical clues (age, exposure, infection history) help infer likely pathways.

t.b: Does the tumour express a targetable protein? Positive HER2 → trastuzumab eligibility; negative HER2 → avoid waste of drug

t.a: PCR or sequencing for hotspot mutations (KRAS, BRAF, EGFR)
t.b: Which targeted agents will work? KRAS wild‑type → EGFR inhibitors possible; KRAS mutant → avoid EGFR inhibitors

t.a: Serology for oncogenic viruses (HBV, HCV, HIV, HPV)
t.b: Is infection driving the cancer? Positive HBV → consider antiviral therapy and surveillance

t.a: If molecular tests unavailable, use clinical risk scores (e.g., WHO HIV‑associated cancer risk) and histology patterns
t.b: Provides a pragmatic treatment plan when labs are limited

b: Targeted therapy: EGFR inhibitors for EGFR‑mutant NSCLC; avoid in KRAS‑mutant disease
Hormone therapy: Tamoxifen for ER‑positive breast cancer; avoid in pre‑menopausal women with thrombotic risk
Immunotherapy: PD‑1 blockers for MSI‑high tumours; contraindicated in active uncontrolled infection
sections.p: Treat the underlying molecular driver when possible, then provide standard cytotoxic or surgical therapy. Supportive care includes pain control, nutrition, and infection prophylaxis.

b: Hyperplasia shows orderly architecture, no invasion, normal p53 staining
Carcinoma shows disorderly cells, invasion, abnormal p53 or Ki‑67
sections.p: Benign proliferative lesions (e.g., hyperplasia) can mimic early cancer histologically but lack invasive growth and molecular driver mutations.

b: A normal p53 IHC does not rule out TP53 mutation (missense vs null)
Negative HPV PCR in cervical cancer may be due to sampling error
sections.p: Low‑grade tumours may have normal Ki‑67; some viral‑associated cancers have low mutation burden yet behave aggressively.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid tumour growth causing airway obstruction, spinal cord compression, or severe bleeding
New onset severe pain, unexplained weight loss, or jaundice in a known cancer patient
